doc.title: Ronnie Zito interviewed by Monk Rowe & Rick Montalbano, via Zoom, March 9, 2022

title: Three Rivers Inn in Syracuse and Tony Riposo teaching him to read
summary: Tony Riposo hired him at 17-18 and taught him to read music by having him sing the parts.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But you were playing gigs around Central New York and the Utica area probably early on.
Well I got a gig in Syracuse at Three Rivers Inn.

Oh yeah. Yeah. And Tony Riposo was the leader and he hired me and at the time I had not much experience playing for acts. And they had big names coming in, you know, Tony Bennett and Sammy Davis, all these people. And I didn’t play for every one. I mean you know most of the big guys had their own rhythm section you know, so I might sit out. But then there were other people that came in like the Mills Brothers, you know, the Maguire Sisters, Four Lads, I would play for them. And it was great experience. And Tony Riposo was the leader. And when I went in there my reading was not — I mean I was about 17 or 18 you know. And my reading was like I told Tony, I says, “Man,” I said, “I don’t know about my reading.” I mean I read music in high school you know, in band, in the band room and concerts. But that was more classical. But Tony said, “Don’t worry about it, don’t worry about it.” I don’t know if you knew Tony well, Rick.
And he said, “Don’t worry about it, I’ll get you through this.” Because Tony just wanted me on the gig because he was a terrific jazz player.
And he just wanted to blow. He wanted to play on the dance sets.

You know he wanted to swing. He wanted to play, and he liked the way I played that you know. That’s kind of how I got the gig. But then he started literally teaching me how to read. You know he’d say, he’d grab a piece of music and he’d say, “Take a look at this,” he goes — or before he would say take a look at it, he’d say, “Can you sing [scats]?” “Can you sing that?” And I would go [scats]. And then Tony would point at the paper and say, “Well that’s what you just sang. It’s on the paper.” He said, “You can do this, you just sang it. If you can sing it, you’ve got a good chance of playing it.” And it was like
that. It was no pressure. He never pressured me or anything like that. Tony Riposo, great musician.
